newsitem.title: EGYPT: Greek artists spend months turning sand into art.
newsitem.headline: Greek artists spend months turning sand into art.

text.p: With the help of earthmovers, loaders and scores of puzzled Egyptian labourers, three Greek women have spent nine months sculpting sand in the Red Sea desert into cones.
Now they intend to watch as nature undoes their efforts, in the space of a few months or years.
"It is a dream that we felt had to happen," said Danae Stratou, who along with cousin Alexandra Stratou and Stella Constantinides make up the D.A.ST art team behind the project.
The women have calculated, levelled and compacted sand with a precision that bordered on the obsessive.
At the weekend dozens of art critics, journalists and labourers meandered through the work's two intertwining spirals of 178 cones as the artists looked on.

"The desert united us and the site, which combines water, the desert, the mountains, gave us inspiration," she told Reuters as strong winds swept round the cones at El-Gouna, hemmed between the Red Sea mountains and the sea some 500 km (310 miles) southeast of Cairo.
"Only in the desert can one experience infinity and nature without artificial constraints," she added.

The artists of D.A.ST -- an acronym for the first initials of their names -- say they will challenge the tools used to measure time, space and distance by recording the erosion of their creation, dubbed Desert Breath.

"Because there is nothing to focus on in the desert you cannot rely on traditional means to determine the shape and scale of things. The horizon is the only point of reference. Perspective becomes altered and we have to adjust our senses to nature. Time becomes clouds that the wind moves," Danae said.
Critics have likened their work to that of artistic duo Christo, whose grandscale projects include wrapping Florida islands with pink plastic and the German parliament in silver.

The two spirals, one of 89 sand cones and one of 89 conical depressions cut into the floor of the desert, circle outwards in different directions in the shape of a nautilus shell, increasing in height and width.
They swirl from a central pool which lies flush with the horizon, which the artists say is the pivot of the work. Mirrors on top of the cones highlight the three-dimensional structure.
The artists say the experience of walking within the installation was central to their conception of Desert Breath.
"It's like inhaling and exhaling. Building up and pulling down," said Alexandra. "That is why we called it Desert Breath."
The largest cone protrusion is 3.75 metres (12 feet) high, the smallest depression 37.5 cm (15 inches) deep.

Constantinides said: "We would spend hours and hours getting the angles just right and making sure that the ratios were the same. Everything was done with a surveying tool to make things level. The workers thought we were mad."
